questions.text: I find that the moral pull of another's pain is something I experience as a direct call to action, not as an abstract consideration.
I frequently reorganize a group's workflow to align with my approach.
When I hear that an unfamiliar person is in pain, I want their situation to improve.
I routinely turn down personal opportunities if they would take me away from people who rely on me.
I keep a maintenance schedule for equipment, subscriptions, and recurring needs.
I tend to miss when someone frames bad news inside good news to soften the blow.
I find that deferring my desires so a group can reach consensus comes easily to me.
I am energized by the process of building a decision together.
When someone raises their voice near me, my whole system goes on high alert.
I routinely turn down favors that would distract from my personal priorities.
I feel a strong pull to finish what I start, even when enthusiasm fades.
I rarely notice when someone slows down a conversation to give a quieter person space to contribute.
I feel little concern for the wellbeing of people I will never meet.
I experience the space between stimulus and response as comfortably wide.
Statistics or reports about people's suffering leave me with little concern for the people involved.
Wanting someone else's suffering to ease rarely crosses my mind.
I feel a strong pull to be deeply involved in important initiatives, though not necessarily in charge.
I often help synthesize multiple perspectives into a direction the group can support.
When something delights me, the delight fills me completely.
I notice the micro-adjustments people make to their clothing or hair when someone they want to impress is nearby.
I notice that I can compartmentalize emotional events and return to whatever I was doing without difficulty.
I have a hard time following when I think I could lead better.
I routinely spend my lunch break helping others with their tasks instead of resting.
I feel most alive when I am working toward my own aspirations.
I find that designing my ideal morning, without accommodation for anyone else, sets me up for success.
I rarely think about what someone left unsaid after a conversation.
I tend to wait until the pressure of a deadline sharpens my focus.
I am attuned to the way social norms shift from one context to another within the same group.
I start projects with what I have and acquire tools as the need becomes clear.
I read whatever catches my interest without following a list.
I naturally claim authority in informal group settings.
I rarely cry, not because I suppress emotions but because they simply don't reach that intensity.
I create backup plans because I know that primary plans sometimes fail.
I am aware of the invisible alliances that form in any group setting.
I notice that my skin flushes or goes pale in direct response to what I'm feeling.
A person's suffering sometimes stays with me after I have left them.
